name: Chinese citizenship by naturalisation

requirements.blocker_text: Chinese permanent residence (the Five-Star Card) is a practical prerequisite before applying for naturalisation, per the National Immigration Administration's own guidance on first-time permanent-residence applications -- Article 7 of the Nationality Law does not state this explicitly, but it is the standard administrative practice.
requirements.fix_path: Obtain Chinese permanent residence first (see cn_permanent_residence or cn_green_card_investor).

requirements.blocker_text: Under Article 7 of the Nationality Law, a foreigner or stateless person willing to abide by China's Constitution and laws may apply for naturalisation if they meet at least one of: being a close relative of a Chinese national, being settled in China, or having another proper reason.
Under Article 8, approval grants Chinese nationality and the applicant may not retain their foreign nationality -- China does not recognise dual nationality under any circumstances (Article 3).

evidence_required.document: Proof of Chinese permanent residence status
Documentation of the qualifying basis (close-relative proof, settlement evidence, or other justification)
Formal renunciation of prior nationality upon approval

sources.title: National Immigration Administration (nia.gov.cn) -- full text of the 中华人民共和国国籍法 (Nationality Law of the People's Republic of China), Articles 3, 7, and 8

notes: China's naturalisation regime is, by a wide margin, the most restrictive settled-category route encountered anywhere in this dataset. Article 7's stated criteria read as unremarkable on paper (close relative of a Chinese national, settled in China, or 'other proper reason') and impose no explicit residence-year requirement at all -- but the Chinese Wikipedia's reproduction of official figures states that from the PRC's founding in 1949 through February 2019, only slightly over 4,000 people successfully naturalised under Article 7 in roughly 70 years, a number small enough that it is sometimes cited alongside individual named cases (e.g. naturalised athletes) rather than as a population statistic. This is a genuinely different kind of restrictiveness than the UAE's or Saudi Arabia's discretionary, uncodified exceptional-merit tracks: China's criteria are written down and look ordinary, but administrative practice makes approval vanishingly rare regardless of how well an applicant matches the stated text -- worth surfacing prominently on this route's detail page precisely because the gap between codified criteria and real-world outcome is so wide. nat_prior_pr is included as a hard requirement despite not appearing explicitly in Article 7 itself, based on secondary reporting (a Baidu-hosted encyclopaedia entry citing '外国人首次申请永久居留指南') that applicants must first hold permanent residence before naturalisation is practically available -- flagged honestly since this specific procedural claim rests on a tier-4 source even though the core statutory text (Articles 3, 7, 8) is fully tier-1 verified via a direct nia.gov.cn fetch. citizenship_after_months = 0 reflects that naturalisation IS citizenship, per this dataset's standard convention -- the real barrier here is nat_prior_pr and the general administrative rarity of approval, not a further waiting period after grant. dual_citizenship_allowed is false with no exceptions documented anywhere in this build's China research, a firmer single-nationality rule than Korea's (which carves out marriage and exceptional-talent exceptions) or Saudi Arabia's (which allows a narrow exception for certain women retaining nationality) -- China's Article 3 states the non-recognition principle with no qualifying language, and Article 8 reinforces it specifically for the naturalisation grant.
